Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.item: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness in a 74-year-old patient, these two appraisals are hard to justify clinically unless the illness clearly resulted from a personally controllable action or omission. 'Intrinsic Fault' and especially 'Inaction Guilt' imply direct responsibility for causing or preventing the event, which is usually implausible for severe illness and would prompt clinical clarification.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, intense self-blame framed as 'not doing more to stop what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there is some specific preventable-action context. The other appraisal items fit illness trauma well ('Body Unreliable', possible social disconnection), but this guilt item implies agency over the trauma in a way that is clinically questionable for the same patient and trauma type.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Body Unreliable' fits a life-threatening illness trauma well, but 'Self-Blame' is hard to reconcile unless the illness was plausibly caused by a specific action or delay attributable to the patient. For most life-threatening illness presentations, this level of direct causal self-blame is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a 74-year-old patient whose trauma type is life-threatening illness, this self-blame item is the only clearly incoherent appraisal. In most illness-related PTSD presentations, especially without any other items suggesting treatment decisions, delay, risky behavior, or preventable exposure, blaming oneself 'because of the way I acted' is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. The other two appraisals about the body being unreliable or acting like danger is ongoing fit illness-related trauma well and are internally consistent with each other, but this self-blame statement pulls toward a different trauma meaning that is not supported anywhere else in the profile.
